query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In fcc-based high-entropy alloys (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi), lowering the intrinsic stacking-fault energy (SFE) via interstitial boron additions promotes mechanical twinning during plastic deformation, which in turn enhances fracture toughness. When SFE is above a critical threshold (~25 mJ/m²), deformation proceeds predominantly by dislocation slip and toughness is limited; reducing SFE below this threshold activates twinning, increasing work hardening and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, homogenized equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy with baseline SFE ≈ 30 mJ/m² and fracture toughness K_IC ≈ 120 MPa·√m at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Systematic addition of interstitial boron from 0 to 0.1 atomic percent to adjust SFE.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a constant strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; specimens electro-polished prior to testing; identical heat‐treatment (1,100 °C/2 h + water quench).
generation.structural_mediator: Stacking-fault energy (mJ/m²) controlling the onset of deformation twinning.
generation.mechanism: Lower SFE increases ease of partial dislocation emission and twin nucleation, promoting a dynamic Hall–Petch effect through twin boundary formation, thereby enhancing strain hardening capacity and fracture resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Boron additions that reduce SFE below ~25 mJ/m² will lead to observable mechanical twins in the microstructure, a ~20–30% increase in work hardening rate, and a corresponding 15–25% increase in fracture toughness relative to baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeMnNi with SFE ≈30 mJ/m², predominantly slip‐controlled deformation, and K_IC ≈120 MPa·√m.
generation.boundary: Holds for fcc single-phase high-entropy alloys with baseline SFE between 20–40 mJ/m²; temperature 200 K–400 K; boron content up to 0.1 at%. Not expected to apply to bcc or hcp high-entropy alloys or to SFE below 15 mJ/m² (where martensitic transformations may dominate).
generation.uncertainty: Moderate; boron may also segregate to grain boundaries and embrittle the alloy at higher concentrations, and the exact SFE threshold for twinning may shift with grain size.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CoCrFeMnNi + B alloys (0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1 at% B), measure SFE via transmission electron microscopy partial dislocation analysis, perform tensile tests with in-situ SEM to quantify twin density and work‐hardening rate, and conduct compact tension tests for fracture toughness.
measurements: True stress–strain curves (to extract work hardening rate)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boron additions do not reduce SFE below ~25 mJ/m² or if reduced SFE does not correlate with increased twin density and enhanced toughness (i.e., no >10% rise in K_IC despite clear twinning), then the hypothesis is falsified.
